questions.question: What is Spring Boot auto-configuration?
questions.title: Spring Boot auto-configuration explained
questions.direct_answer: Auto-configuration is Spring Boot's mechanism that automatically creates and configures beans based on what's on the classpath and what properties are set. If spring-data-jpa is on the classpath and a datasource URL is in properties, Boot auto-configures a JPA EntityManagerFactory, transaction manager, and repositories — without you writing any of that configuration.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands that auto-configuration is a conditional bean creation mechanism, not just 'magic' that happens automatically.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers say 'Spring Boot does everything automatically' without understanding the classpath scanning and conditional logic that drives which beans get created.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention a specific @Conditional annotation like @ConditionalOnClass and explain how it checks the classpath before creating beans — shows you've looked under the hood.

sections.title: Spring Boot's Smart Bean Creation System
sections.content:
**Auto-configuration** is Spring Boot setting up beans for you, based on what it finds. You add a library, Spring Boot looks at it, and it wires the objects you'd normally write by hand.

Why it exists: a plain Spring app makes you declare every bean yourself — the datasource, the transaction manager, the JSON converter. That's a lot of boilerplate. Auto-configuration hands you sensible defaults instead, so you start with working infrastructure on day one.

How it works: Spring Boot ships hundreds of small configuration classes. `@SpringBootApplication` turns them on through `@EnableAutoConfiguration`. Each class is guarded by a condition, and the common ones are:

- `@ConditionalOnClass` — run only if a given class is on the classpath.
- `@ConditionalOnProperty` — run only if a property is set.
- `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` — back off if you already defined that bean.

The nuance interviewers want: it isn't magic, it's **conditional**. Every bean has a gate, and the gate is checked at startup. Add the H2 driver plus a datasource URL and the JDBC auto-config fires; leave them out and it stays quiet.

> **The gotcha:** auto-configuration is deterministic, not guesswork. Run with `--debug` to see the exact conditions that passed or failed.

blue|Conditional, not magic|~Gated bean creation|every bean has conditions|deterministic decision tree|fails fast on startup

sections.title: How Auto-Configuration Creates Beans Conditionally
When Auto-Configuration Helps Most
sections.content: Use auto-configuration when building standard enterprise applications where you want **rapid development without boilerplate**. It shines when you're creating REST APIs with database access — add spring-boot-starter-web and spring-boot-starter-data-jpa, and you get an embedded Tomcat server, Jackson JSON converter, Hibernate ORM, and connection pooling configured together. Perfect for microservices where each service needs database, logging, metrics, and health checks but you don't want to spend days configuring infrastructure. Also ideal for prototypes and MVPs where time-to-demo matters more than custom infrastructure. The pattern works because most Java applications need the same 80% of infrastructure — datasources, web servers, security, logging — and only differ in the 20% business logic.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking It's Pure Magic**: Freshers say 'Spring Boot just does everything' without realizing there's a decision tree of @Conditional checks happening at startup. Every auto-configured bean has conditions that must be satisfied — it's deterministic logic, not guesswork.
- **Fighting Auto-Configuration Instead of Disabling It**: When auto-configuration does something unwanted, freshers try to override it by creating competing beans or setting obscure properties, causing conflicts. The clean approach is to exclude that auto-config class entirely using @SpringBootApplication(exclude).
- **Not Checking What Got Auto-Configured**: Freshers assume beans exist without verifying. Use the /actuator/conditions endpoint or --debug flag to see exactly which auto-configurations activated and why others didn't.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@Conditional annotations**: Drive auto-configuration by checking classpath, properties, and existing beans before creating new ones
- **Classpath scanning**: Auto-configuration activates based on what JARs are present — add spring-kafka, get Kafka beans automatically
- **Property-driven behavior**: Many auto-configs read application.properties to customize bean creation without code changes
- **ConditionalOnMissingBean**: Allows your bean definitions to override Boot's defaults — your beans are created first, Boot's conditions see them and back off
- **Starter dependencies**: Each starter like spring-boot-starter-web bundles related auto-configurations that work together
- **Fail-fast validation**: If conditions aren't met (like missing driver class), Boot fails at startup with a clear error, not at runtime
- **Debug mode**: Run with --debug flag to see a condition evaluation report showing which auto-configs activated and why

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Auto-configuration is Spring Boot's conditional bean creation system. It looks at your classpath and properties, then creates the beans you need automatically. Here's how it works: when you add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa to your project, Spring Boot sees the JPA classes on the classpath and checks if you've provided a database URL in your properties file. If both conditions are met, it auto-configures an EntityManagerFactory, a transaction manager, and enables repository scanning — everything you need for database access. The key word is conditional. Every auto-configuration class uses annotations like at-ConditionalOnClass or at-ConditionalOnProperty to check whether it should activate. If you add the H2 database driver, Boot sees it and configures an embedded database. If you define your own DataSource bean, Boot's at-ConditionalOnMissingBean check detects it and skips the auto-configured version. That's how Spring Boot gives you smart defaults but lets you override anything. One thing freshers miss: this isn't magic or guessing. It's a deterministic decision tree. You can see exactly what got auto-configured by running your app with the debug flag or hitting the actuator conditions endpoint. That report shows which auto-configs activated and which didn't, along with the reasons. Understanding this separation between conditions and bean creation is what separates someone who uses Spring Boot from someone who understands it.

speakable_v2.hook: Auto-configuration isn't magic. It's hundreds of small config classes that only switch on when the right conditions are met.

beats.text: Auto-configuration is Spring Boot wiring up beans for you, based on what's on the classpath. You add a library and starters bring in opinionated defaults, so you don't write that setup by hand. It's conditional, though, not truly automatic.

Plain Spring makes you declare every bean yourself. That's a pile of boilerplate for things every app needs. Auto-configuration hands you working defaults instead, so on day one you've already got a datasource and a web server.

@ConditionalOnProperty fires it only when a property is set.
@ConditionalOnMissingBean tells Boot to back off if you already defined that bean.

Not checking what fired. Run with the debug flag and read the conditions report.

questions.question: How does Spring Boot know which auto-configurations to apply?
questions.title: Auto-configuration discovery mechanism
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot reads a file — spring.factories in Boot 2 or AutoConfiguration.imports in Boot 3 — inside each starter JAR. This file lists all available auto-configuration classes. Spring Boot loads them all at startup, but each one's @Conditional annotations determine which actually activate. Only those with satisfied conditions create beans.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the discovery mechanism — how Spring Boot finds auto-configuration classes in the first place, not just how they work once found.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers think Spring Boot scans all classes for @Configuration, missing the fact that auto-configs are explicitly registered in a metadata file.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Boot 2 to Boot 3 migration from spring.factories to AutoConfiguration.imports and explain why the change happened (faster startup, better modularity).

sections.title: The Auto-Configuration Discovery Process
sections.content:
**Spring Boot discovers auto-configurations from a manifest file**, not by scanning every class. At startup it opens each JAR on the classpath and reads one special file that lists the auto-configuration classes that JAR provides.

Why a file: scanning thousands of classes across dozens of JARs would be slow. A plain list is fast to read and easy to ship inside a library.

How it works: the file location depends on the version.

- Boot 2 used `META-INF/spring.factories`, a key-value format.
- Boot 3 uses `META-INF/spring/...AutoConfiguration.imports`, a simple one-class-per-line list.

Spring Boot loads every class named in those files, then checks each class's `@Conditional` gates. Loading isn't the same as activating — a class can be listed yet still back off because its conditions fail.

The nuance: discovery and activation are two phases. The manifest decides what counts as a *candidate*; the conditions decide what actually runs.

> **The gotcha:** if you build a custom starter and forget the imports file, your auto-config never loads — Spring Boot simply can't see it.

sections.title: How Spring Boot Discovers Auto-Configurations
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A[Application starts] --> B[Scan every JAR on the classpath] B --> C[Read META-INF
AutoConfiguration.imports] C --> D[Load every listed
auto-config class] D --> E{Evaluate @Conditional
on each class} E -->|conditions pass| F[Create beans] E -->|conditions fail| G[Skip silently] F --> H[ApplicationContext ready] G --> H ``` *Discovery loads all candidates from the manifest file; the `@Conditional` checks decide which actually activate.*

sections.title: AutoConfiguration.imports File and How It Works
When This Discovery Mechanism Matters
sections.content: Understanding the discovery mechanism matters when you're **building custom starters** or **debugging why an auto-config isn't activating**. If you create a company-wide starter for common database configurations, you must create an AutoConfiguration.imports file listing your auto-config classes — Boot won't find them otherwise. When an expected bean isn't being created, check if the auto-config class is even listed in the metadata file. Sometimes Maven shade or fat JAR plugins break this file during packaging by overwriting it instead of merging entries from multiple JARs. The discovery mechanism also explains startup performance: Boot 3 switched to AutoConfiguration.imports because it's faster to parse than the key-value format of spring.factories. For troubleshooting, run with --debug to see Boot's condition evaluation report showing which auto-configs were considered and which conditions failed.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming Classpath Scanning**: Freshers think Spring Boot scans all classes for @Configuration annotations, which would be slow with hundreds of JARs. The reality is Boot only loads classes explicitly listed in AutoConfiguration.imports files.
- **Forgetting the Metadata File**: When creating custom auto-configurations, freshers write the @Configuration class but forget to create the AutoConfiguration.imports file, then wonder why their auto-config never runs.
- **Not Understanding Boot 2 vs Boot 3**: The file name and format changed — spring.factories used a key=value format, AutoConfiguration.imports is a simple list. If you're reading Boot 2 tutorials and working in Boot 3, you'll look in the wrong file.
- **Ignoring Condition Evaluation**: Just because a class is listed in AutoConfiguration.imports doesn't mean it activates. Freshers see a class in the file and assume its beans exist, missing that the @Conditional checks might have failed.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Metadata file**: AutoConfiguration.imports in Boot 3, spring.factories in Boot 2 — explicitly lists all auto-configuration classes, no scanning
- **Discovery vs activation**: Boot loads all listed classes but only activates those with satisfied @Conditional annotations
- **Performance optimization**: Using a metadata file is faster than scanning every class in every JAR on the classpath
- **Custom starters**: To create your own, write auto-config classes AND list them in META-INF/spring/AutoConfiguration.imports
- **Boot 3 migration**: Changed from spring.factories key-value format to AutoConfiguration.imports plain list for faster parsing and better modularity
- **Condition evaluation report**: Run with --debug flag to see which auto-configs were loaded and which conditions passed or failed
- **JAR packaging issues**: Fat JAR plugins can break auto-configuration by overwriting metadata files instead of merging them from all JARs

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Spring Boot uses a metadata file to discover auto-configuration classes, not classpath scanning. When your application starts, Boot looks inside every JAR on the classpath for a file called AutoConfiguration.imports in the META-INF/spring directory. This file contains a list of fully-qualified class names, one per line. For example, the main spring-boot-autoconfigure JAR has an AutoConfiguration.imports file that lists over 150 auto-configuration classes like DataSourceAutoConfiguration and WebMvcAutoConfiguration. Boot reads all these files from all JARs and loads every class mentioned. That's the discovery phase. But loading doesn't mean activating. Each auto-configuration class has at-Conditional annotations that check conditions like whether certain classes are on the classpath or whether properties are set. Only auto-configs with all conditions satisfied actually create beans. This two-phase approach is much faster than scanning every single class in every JAR looking for at-Configuration annotations. One thing that changed in Spring Boot 3: the metadata file used to be called spring.factories and used a key-value format. Boot 3 switched to AutoConfiguration.imports with a simpler list format because it's faster to parse and more modular. If you're creating a custom starter, you have to create this file and list your auto-config classes in it — otherwise Boot will never find them. This is a common mistake: freshers write the auto-configuration class but forget the metadata file, then can't figure out why their beans aren't being created.

speakable_v2.hook: Spring Boot doesn't guess which configs to apply. It reads a manifest baked into every starter JAR.
speakable_v2.familiarity_override_reason: This question is about the discovery manifest, not the JPA starter stack, so the codex datasource example doesn't fit.

Scanning thousands of classes across dozens of JARs would be slow. A flat list is quick to read and easy to ship inside a library. So Boot trades scanning for a simple lookup.

questions.question: How do you disable a specific Spring Boot auto-configuration?
questions.title: Disabling Spring Boot auto-configuration
questions.direct_answer: Use exclude on @SpringBootApplication: @SpringBootApplication(exclude = {DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class}). Or in properties: spring.autoconfigure.exclude=org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration. Useful when Boot auto-configures something you want to control manually.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows how to take control when auto-configuration does something unwanted — practical skill for real projects.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers try to fight auto-configuration by creating competing beans, causing conflicts, instead of cleanly disabling the auto-config first.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention a real scenario where you'd exclude an auto-config, like excluding DataSourceAutoConfiguration when using multiple datasources or a custom connection pool library.

sections.title: Taking Control from Auto-Configuration
sections.content:
**Disabling an auto-configuration** tells Spring Boot to skip one of its setup classes, so none of that class's beans get created.

Why you'd want this: sometimes Boot configures something you don't want. Maybe it builds a datasource when you run multiple databases yourself, or it sets up default security you plan to replace.

How it works: there are two clean ways.

- Annotation: `@SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)` — checked at compile time, visible in code.
- Property: `spring.autoconfigure.exclude=...` in `application.properties` — switchable per environment, no recompile.

Both stop the class before it runs a single `@Bean` method.

The nuance: **excluding is cleaner than fighting**. Defining a competing bean lets Boot's bean get created first, which wastes resources or clashes. Exclusion removes it at the source.

> **The gotcha:** excluding one auto-config can cascade. Drop `DataSourceAutoConfiguration` and JPA, which depends on it, quietly stops working too.

sections.title: Disabling an Auto-Configuration at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Why exclude|~Take control|Boot configured something unwanted|multi-datasource, custom security|cleaner than competing beans
blue|Annotation way|~Compile-time checked|@SpringBootApplication(exclude=...)|DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class|visible in code
emerald|Property way|~Per-environment|spring.autoconfigure.exclude|fully-qualified class name|no recompile needed
rose|Cascade warning|~Dependents break too|exclude DataSource|JPA and JdbcTemplate also drop|verify with --debug

sections.title: Step 1: Identify the Auto-Configuration Class to Exclude
sections.content: First, find the exact auto-configuration class causing the problem. Run your application with --debug flag to see the condition evaluation report, which lists all active auto-configurations. Look for the one creating unwanted beans. Common culprits: DataSourceAutoConfiguration creates datasource beans, SecurityAutoConfiguration sets up default security, JmxAutoConfiguration enables JMX monitoring, and ErrorMvcAutoConfiguration creates the default error page. You need the fully-qualified class name. For example, if Boot is trying to create a datasource but you're using MongoDB only, you'd identify org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration as the class to exclude. Check the Spring Boot documentation's auto-configuration reference appendix for a complete list of auto-config classes and what they do.

sections.title: Excluding an Auto-Configuration in Code
Step 2: Choose Exclusion Method Based on Your Needs
sections.content: Use **annotation-based exclusion** when the decision is permanent and code-visible. Add exclude to @SpringBootApplication: @SpringBootApplication(exclude = {DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class, JmxAutoConfiguration.class}). This works at compile time, so typos cause compilation errors. Use **property-based exclusion** when you need environment-specific control or when modifying code isn't convenient. In application.properties: spring.autoconfigure.exclude=org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration,org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jmx.JmxAutoConfiguration. This approach lets you exclude different auto-configs in dev versus prod by using profile-specific properties files. Property-based exclusion is also useful in test configurations where you want to disable certain infrastructure like scheduled tasks or async processing.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Creating Competing Beans**: Freshers see an unwanted auto-configured bean and try to fix it by creating their own bean with @Primary, but the auto-configured beans already exist and consume resources or cause conflicts during startup. Clean exclusion prevents the beans from being created at all.
- **Excluding Too Broadly**: Disabling DataSourceAutoConfiguration when you actually just want to customize the connection pool. Often you can achieve what you want by defining your own bean (like a custom DataSource) and letting @ConditionalOnMissingBean skip Boot's default, without excluding the entire auto-config.
- **Wrong Class Name in Properties**: When using property-based exclusion, freshers use the simple class name or typo the package, and the exclusion silently fails because Boot can't find that class. Use fully-qualified names and check for typos.
- **Not Understanding Cascading Dependencies**: Excluding one auto-config can break others that depend on its beans. For example, excluding DataSourceAutoConfiguration will also break JpaAutoConfiguration, which needs a datasource.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Annotation exclusion**: @SpringBootApplication(exclude = {ClassName.class}) — compile-time checked, visible in code, good for permanent decisions
- **Property exclusion**: spring.autoconfigure.exclude=fully.qualified.ClassName in application.properties — runtime, environment-specific, useful for testing
- **Multiple exclusions**: Both methods support multiple classes, separated by comma in properties or as array elements in annotation
- **Debug flag**: Run with --debug to see condition evaluation report showing which auto-configs are active and what they created
- **Cascading effects**: Excluding one auto-config can disable dependent auto-configs — excluding DataSourceAutoConfiguration disables JPA and JDBC template configs
- **Better than fighting**: Exclusion is cleaner than creating competing beans with @Primary, which can cause conflicts and waste resources
- **Real scenarios**: Disable DataSource auto-config for multi-datasource apps, disable Security auto-config in development, disable JMX in containerized deployments

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: You disable an auto-configuration by excluding it, which tells Spring Boot to completely skip that configuration class. There are two ways to do this. The first is annotation-based: you add the exclude attribute to your at-SpringBootApplication annotation. For example, at-SpringBootApplication with exclude equals DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class. The second is property-based: in your application.properties file, you set spring.autoconfigure.exclude equal to the fully-qualified class name like org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration. Both do the same thing — they prevent that auto-config class from running its at-Bean methods. I'd use the annotation approach when the exclusion is permanent and should be visible in code. I'd use the property approach when I need environment-specific behavior, like disabling security auto-config in development but keeping it in production. A real scenario where you'd do this is when you're configuring multiple datasources. Spring Boot's DataSourceAutoConfiguration assumes a single datasource, so if you're building a multi-tenant app with dynamic datasource routing, you'd exclude DataSourceAutoConfiguration and set up your own datasource beans with custom routing logic. One mistake freshers make is trying to fight auto-configuration by creating competing beans instead of just disabling the auto-config cleanly. That causes conflicts because the auto-configured beans still get created. Another mistake is excluding the wrong class or using a typo in the property, and the exclusion silently fails. Always verify by running with the debug flag and checking the condition evaluation report to confirm the auto-config you wanted to exclude didn't activate.

speakable_v2.familiarity_override_reason: This question is about turning auto-config off, while the codex starter example shows the opposite, so it doesn't fit.

beats.text: Disabling an auto-configuration tells Spring Boot to skip one setup class completely. Starters bring in opinionated defaults, and sometimes one of those defaults isn't what you want. Excluding it means none of its beans get created.
Maybe Boot builds a datasource when you manage databases yourself. Maybe it adds default security you plan to replace. Turning the class off is cleaner than fighting the beans it creates.

items: Annotation: @SpringBootApplication with exclude, checked at compile time.
Property: spring.autoconfigure.exclude in application.properties, switchable per environment.
Both stop the class before it runs a single bean method.

Typing the wrong class name in the property, so the exclusion silently does nothing.

questions.question: What is @ConditionalOnMissingBean and how does it enable overriding auto-configuration?
questions.title: @ConditionalOnMissingBean — user beans take priority
questions.direct_answer: @ConditionalOnMissingBean means: only create this bean if the application context doesn't already have a bean of that type. This lets Spring Boot provide a default bean (auto-configured), while allowing you to override it by defining your own bean of the same type. Your bean wins because Boot's @ConditionalOnMissingBean check sees yours and skips the auto-configured version.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the override mechanism that makes Spring Boot's 'opinionated defaults with easy customization' possible.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers define their own bean but don't realize user-defined beans are processed before auto-configuration, which is why @ConditionalOnMissingBean works — they think it's random ordering.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that user @Configuration classes are processed before auto-configuration classes, so your bean always exists first when the condition check runs — shows understanding of Spring Boot's configuration phases.

sections.title: Spring Boot's Override Mechanism
sections.content:
**`@ConditionalOnMissingBean`** is a rule that says: create this bean only if one of that type isn't already there. It's the switch that lets your beans win over Spring Boot's defaults.

Why it exists: Spring Boot wants to give you working defaults without trapping you. This condition makes its defaults polite — they step aside the moment you supply your own.

How it works: it comes down to ordering. Spring processes your `@Configuration` classes first, so your beans exist early. Auto-configuration runs later. By the time Boot checks `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`, your bean is already in the context, the condition fails, and Boot skips its version.

- Define your own `DataSource` and Boot's default datasource backs off.
- Skip it, and you get Boot's sensible default instead.

The nuance: it matches by type, including subtypes. A `HikariDataSource` bean satisfies a check for `DataSource`.

> **The gotcha:** you don't need `@Primary` to override an auto-configured bean. The condition already stops Boot's bean from being created.

sections.title: @ConditionalOnMissingBean at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|The rule|~Create only if absent|@ConditionalOnMissingBean|checks the context by type|Boot's default backs off
blue|Processing order|~User config runs first|your @Configuration beans|then auto-config classes|your bean already exists
emerald|Override mechanism|~Define your own bean|same type wins|no @Primary needed|the condition fails for Boot
violet|Type matching|~By type and subtype|HikariDataSource satisfies DataSource|matches the hierarchy|debug shows the skip

sections.title: Overriding an Auto-Configured Bean
When to Use ConditionalOnMissingBean
sections.content: Use @ConditionalOnMissingBean when you're **building custom starter libraries** or **shared configuration modules** that provide sensible defaults but should be easily overridable. For example, if you create a company-wide logging starter, you'd configure a default log format and appenders with @ConditionalOnMissingBean, allowing individual teams to override the log format by defining their own bean. In application code, you rarely use this annotation directly — you just define your bean and let Spring Boot's auto-configs detect it via their @ConditionalOnMissingBean checks. The pattern works for any infrastructure bean: datasources, connection pools, message converters, transaction managers, security filters, cache managers. Any time you want to provide a working default that developers can replace by simply defining their own bean without complex configuration ordering or @Primary tricks.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not Understanding Processing Order**: Freshers define a bean to override Boot's default, but don't realize why it works. They think it's random or that @Primary is required. The truth: user @Configuration classes are always processed before auto-configurations, so your bean always exists first when the condition check runs.
- **Using @Primary Unnecessarily**: Freshers add @Primary to their bean thinking it's needed to override the auto-configured one, but @ConditionalOnMissingBean already prevents the auto-configured bean from being created. @Primary is only needed when you have multiple beans of the same type and want to mark one as default.
- **Wrong Bean Type in Condition**: If the auto-config checks @ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class) but you define a bean with a specific implementation type like HikariDataSource, the condition sees it because HikariDataSource is a DataSource. But if the condition checks for a specific type and you provide a different implementation, the condition won't see it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Condition semantics**: @ConditionalOnMissingBean checks if application context contains a bean of specified type before creating a new one
- **Processing order**: User @Configuration classes run before auto-configuration classes, ensuring your beans exist when Boot checks conditions
- **Override mechanism**: Define your own bean of the same type, Boot's @ConditionalOnMissingBean sees it and skips creating the default
- **No @Primary needed**: You don't need @Primary to override auto-configured beans — the condition prevents Boot's bean from being created at all
- **Type matching**: Condition matches by type and subtypes — defining HikariDataSource satisfies @ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)
- **Multiple beans**: @ConditionalOnMissingBean can check for multiple types, requiring all to be missing before creating the bean
- **Debug visibility**: With --debug flag, condition evaluation report shows when @ConditionalOnMissingBean conditions fail because a bean exists

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: At-ConditionalOnMissingBean is an annotation that says: only create this bean if there isn't already a bean of that type in the application context. Spring Boot uses this on almost all auto-configured beans to let you override them. Here's how it works: when you start your application, Spring first processes your at-Configuration classes and creates all your custom beans. Then it loads auto-configuration classes and evaluates their conditions. By the time Boot checks at-ConditionalOnMissingBean on an auto-configured bean, your bean already exists, so the condition fails and Boot skips creating its default. For example, DataSourceAutoConfiguration has at-ConditionalOnMissingBean on its dataSource method. If you define your own DataSource bean in your configuration, Boot sees it and doesn't create the auto-configured one. Your bean wins. This is why Spring Boot can provide opinionated defaults for everything while still letting you customize anything — it's not magic, it's deliberate ordering. User configuration always runs before auto-configuration. One thing freshers get wrong: they think you need at-Primary to override an auto-configured bean, but you don't. The at-ConditionalOnMissingBean check prevents Boot's bean from being created in the first place. at-Primary is only needed when you have multiple beans of the same type and want to mark one as the default choice. Another thing to understand: the condition matches by type hierarchy. If Boot checks at-ConditionalOnMissingBean with DataSource.class, and you define a HikariDataSource bean, the condition sees it because HikariDataSource is a DataSource. This is the core mechanism that makes Spring Boot both convenient and flexible.

Boot wants to give you defaults without locking you in. This condition makes those defaults polite. The moment you supply your own bean, Boot's version steps aside.

Auto-configuration runs later and checks the condition.
It matches by type, so a HikariDataSource satisfies a check for DataSource.

questions.question: What is the Spring Boot auto-configuration report and how do you read it?
questions.title: Spring Boot conditions evaluation report
questions.direct_answer: The auto-configuration report (conditions evaluation report) is a detailed diagnostic log that shows which auto-configurations applied and which didn't during Spring Boot startup. You trigger it by running with --debug flag or setting debug=true in application.properties. It's the primary debugging tool for understanding why expected beans aren't being created.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the single most important diagnostic tool for Spring Boot configuration problems, which separates effective debuggers from those who guess randomly.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers don't know this report exists and spend hours adding random dependencies or changing properties blindly, never checking what conditions actually failed.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate reading the Negative matches section first when debugging, identify the specific failed condition like ConditionalOnClass, and explain how you'd trace backward to find the missing dependency or property that caused it.

sections.title: What the Auto-Configuration Report Shows You
sections.content:
**The conditions evaluation report** is Spring Boot's startup log of which auto-configurations applied and which didn't. It's your map when a bean you expected never showed up.

Why it exists: with hundreds of conditional classes, you can't guess why one didn't fire. The report prints the decision for each one, with the reason.

How to turn it on: set `debug=true` in `application.properties`, or run with the `--debug` flag. The report then prints in three parts.

- **Positive matches** — what activated, and which condition passed.
- **Negative matches** — what didn't, and the exact condition that failed.
- **Exclusions** — what you switched off yourself.

The nuance: when debugging, jump to negative matches first. A line like `@ConditionalOnClass did not find` points straight at a missing dependency.

> **The gotcha:** most freshers never enable this report and guess for hours. The answer is usually sitting in the negative matches.

sections.title: Reading the Conditions Report at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Enable it|~Turn on the report|debug=true in properties|or the --debug flag|prints at startup
emerald|Positive matches|~What activated|auto-config + passed conditions|builds your mental model|see what Boot configured
rose|Negative matches|~The debugging goldmine|what did NOT activate|the exact failed condition|missing class or property
blue|Read it right|~Go to negatives first|find your expected config|fix the named cause|no random guessing

sections.title: Enabling and Reading the Report
Step 1: Check Positive Matches First
sections.content: When the application works as expected, scan the **Positive matches** section to understand what Spring Boot actually configured for you. Each entry shows the auto-configuration class name (like DataSourceAutoConfiguration) and the specific conditions that passed (like @ConditionalOnClass found the H2 driver). This builds your mental model of what's running. For a typical REST API, you'd see JacksonAutoConfiguration, WebMvcAutoConfiguration, DataSourceAutoConfiguration in this section. If you're debugging and something IS working when you expected it not to, this section reveals the auto-configuration you forgot was active.

sections.title: Step 2: Debug with Negative Matches
sections.content: When a feature isn't working, go straight to **Negative matches**. This section lists every auto-configuration that was considered but rejected, with the exact reason. Look for the configuration you expected to fire. Common patterns: "Did not match: @ConditionalOnClass did not find required class 'com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver'" means you forgot the MySQL dependency in pom.xml. "Did not match: @ConditionalOnProperty (spring.datasource.url) did not find property 'spring.datasource.url'" means you forgot to configure the database URL. The failed condition tells you exactly what's missing — no guessing required. This is where freshers save hours of frustration by reading instead of randomly trying fixes.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not enabling the report**: Freshers try to debug Spring Boot configuration issues by adding random @Bean definitions or dependencies without ever looking at the report, turning a 5-minute fix into a 2-hour ordeal.
- **Reading only Positive matches**: When debugging a missing feature, freshers scroll through what worked instead of jumping to Negative matches where the answer is.
- **Ignoring the exact condition message**: The report says "did not find required class 'org.hibernate.SessionFactory'" but freshers add the wrong dependency (like hibernate-core instead of hibernate-jpa) because they didn't read the full class name carefully.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Conditions evaluation report**: diagnostic log showing which auto-configurations applied (Positive), which didn't (Negative), and which were excluded
- **Enable with debug=true**: add to application.properties or use --debug command line flag, report prints to console during startup
- **Positive matches**: lists auto-configurations that applied and the conditions that passed, useful for understanding what Spring Boot configured automatically
- **Negative matches**: the debugging goldmine — shows failed auto-configurations and the exact condition that failed (missing class, property, or bean)
- **ConditionalOnClass failures**: most common in Negative matches, indicates missing Maven/Gradle dependency for that library
- **ConditionalOnProperty failures**: indicates missing or misconfigured property in application.properties or application.yml
- **Read Negative matches first**: when debugging, go directly to this section and find your expected auto-configuration to see why it didn't fire

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The auto-configuration report is Spring Boot's diagnostic tool that shows exactly what happened during startup. You enable it by adding debug equals true to application dot properties or running with the dash dash debug flag. The report has three main sections. Positive matches lists all the auto-configurations that applied and why — like it'll say DataSourceAutoConfiguration matched because ConditionalOnClass found the H2 driver. Negative matches is the debugging section — it shows auto-configurations that were evaluated but didn't apply, with the exact reason. If you expected Redis support but it's not working, you'd see RedisAutoConfiguration in Negative matches with a message like did not find required class RedisOperations, which tells you the spring-boot-starter-data-redis dependency is missing. The third section is Exclusions, which lists auto-configurations you explicitly turned off. When I'm debugging why a feature isn't working, I go straight to Negative matches and search for the relevant auto-configuration. The failed condition usually points directly to the fix — either a missing dependency, a misconfigured property, or a bean that wasn't created. One mistake freshers make is not enabling this report at all and just randomly trying fixes. The report gives you the answer in seconds instead of hours of guessing. It's like having X-ray vision into Spring Boot's decision-making process.

questions.question: What is @ConditionalOnProperty and when do you use it?
questions.title: @ConditionalOnProperty for feature flags
questions.direct_answer: ConditionalOnProperty is a Spring Boot annotation that creates a bean only when a specific property exists in application.properties or application.yml, optionally with a specific value. It's used for feature flags — enabling or disabling functionality through configuration without code changes. For example, you can conditionally enable a batch job or mock service based on a property.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands property-driven conditional bean creation, a practical pattern for runtime configuration flexibility.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers create beans unconditionally and put if-else logic inside the bean to check properties at runtime, instead of letting Spring decide whether to create the bean in the first place based on configuration.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete real-world example like conditionally enabling a scheduled job in production only, or using a mock payment gateway in dev mode but the real one in production, controlled purely by application properties.

sections.title: Property-Driven Bean Creation
sections.content:
**`@ConditionalOnProperty`** creates a bean only when a chosen property is set, optionally to a chosen value. It's how you build a feature flag in plain Spring Boot.

Why it exists: you often want a bean in one environment but not another — a real payment gateway in prod, a mock in dev. Checking the property inside the bean still builds the bean. This condition skips building it at all.

How it works: three small knobs.

- `name` — the property key to look at.
- `havingValue` — the value it must equal.
- `matchIfMissing` — what to do when the key is absent.

So `@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "app.cache.enabled", havingValue = "true")` makes the bean exist only when that property is `true`.

The nuance: because the bean never gets created, there's no wasted memory and no dead branch to maintain.

> **The gotcha:** always set `matchIfMissing` on purpose. Leave it out and the behaviour when the key is missing can surprise you.

sections.title: @ConditionalOnProperty at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|What it does|~Property-driven switch|create bean only if property set|optional havingValue|a real feature flag
blue|Parameters|~Three knobs|name = the key|havingValue = expected value|matchIfMissing = absent behavior
emerald|Why better|~Bean never created|no wasted memory or CPU|cleaner than if-else inside|decided at startup
violet|Real uses|~Per-environment beans|mock gateway in dev|scheduler only in prod|toggle without redeploy

sections.title: Feature Flag with ConditionalOnProperty
When to Use ConditionalOnProperty
sections.content: Use ConditionalOnProperty when you need environment-specific behavior without code changes. **Scheduled jobs** that should run only in production (app.scheduler.enabled=true in prod, false in dev). **Mock external services** for development where you'd use a fake email sender or payment gateway (app.email.mock=true in dev, false in prod). **Optional features** that customers can toggle like premium analytics or advanced reporting (app.features.analytics=true). **Performance-heavy beans** like caching layers or connection pools that you want to disable in local development (app.cache.enabled=true in prod). **Debugging tools** like custom health checks or metrics exporters that should only exist in certain environments. The key insight: if you find yourself writing if-else checks on properties inside beans, consider using ConditionalOnProperty instead to not create the bean at all.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Checking properties inside beans**: Freshers create a bean unconditionally and then check properties with at-Value inside the bean's methods, using if-statements for every operation. This wastes memory and CPU on code that never runs. Use ConditionalOnProperty to prevent bean creation entirely.
- **Forgetting matchIfMissing**: The annotation requires explicit true or false for matchIfMissing parameter. If omitted and the property is missing, Spring's behavior is undefined. Always specify matchIfMissing equals false if you want the bean skipped when the property is absent.
- **Not testing both conditions**: Freshers set the property to true in application.properties and test, but never test with it false or missing, so they don't notice they have two beans fighting for the same interface.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **ConditionalOnProperty**: annotation that creates a bean only when a specific property exists in application.properties or application.yml
- **name parameter**: the property key to check (e.g. name equals "app.scheduler.enabled")
- **havingValue parameter**: optional specific value the property must match (e.g. havingValue equals "true"), if omitted the bean is created when property exists with any non-false value
- **matchIfMissing parameter**: controls behavior when property is absent — matchIfMissing equals true creates the bean when property is missing, false skips it
- **Feature flags**: primary use case, enabling or disabling functionality through configuration without code changes
- **Environment-specific beans**: use to create mock services in dev but real services in prod, controlled by properties per environment
- **Prevents bean creation**: more efficient than creating the bean and checking properties inside with if-statements — no wasted resources

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: ConditionalOnProperty is an annotation that tells Spring Boot to create a bean only if a specific property exists in your configuration files. You put it on a bean method or configuration class along with the property name to check. For example, if you have a scheduled job that should only run in production, you'd annotate it with ConditionalOnProperty name equals app dot scheduler dot enabled, havingValue equals true. Then in your production application dot properties you'd set that property to true, and in dev you'd set it to false or just leave it out. Spring checks this at startup — if the condition passes, it creates the bean, otherwise it skips it completely. This is way better than creating the bean always and then checking the property value inside with if-statements. The bean never wastes memory or CPU if it's not needed. A real example I'd use: conditionally enabling a mock payment gateway in dev mode. You'd have two bean methods, both returning PaymentGateway interface. One has ConditionalOnProperty for app dot payment dot mock equals true and returns a fake implementation. The other checks for false and returns the real Stripe integration. In dev you'd set the property to true and get instant fake responses. In prod you'd set it false and hit the real API. One mistake freshers make is not specifying the matchIfMissing parameter. If you want the bean skipped when the property is missing entirely, you must set matchIfMissing equals false explicitly. Otherwise Spring's behavior isn't guaranteed. This pattern is super practical for feature flags and environment-specific configuration.

You often want a bean in one environment but not another. A real payment gateway in prod, a mock in dev. Checking the property inside the bean still builds it. This skips building it at all.

havingValue is the value it must match.

questions.question: How does Spring Boot's auto-configuration relate to Spring profiles?
questions.title: Auto-configuration and Spring profiles
questions.direct_answer: Auto-configuration and profiles are complementary mechanisms that work together. Auto-configuration activates beans based on structural conditions like classpath contents and existing beans (ConditionalOnClass, ConditionalOnBean). Profiles activate beans based on the active environment (dev, test, prod) using at-Profile annotation. You combine them: auto-configuration provides the default setup, profiles customize it per environment. Set active profiles via spring.profiles.active property.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands how two core Spring Boot mechanisms interact and when to reach for each tool.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers think profiles and auto-configuration are competing alternatives or conflate them into one concept, not realizing they solve different problems — structural setup versus environment-specific customization.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe a concrete scenario combining both: Spring Boot auto-configures a DataSource if it finds database drivers, but you use at-Profile on your custom DataSource beans to have H2 in dev, Postgres in test, and MySQL in prod, all working together.

sections.title: Two Complementary Configuration Layers
sections.content:
**Auto-configuration and profiles are two different layers** that work together. Auto-configuration asks a structural question — what's on the classpath? Profiles ask an environmental one — which environment am I in?

Why both exist: auto-configuration gives you a working framework from your dependencies. Profiles let that framework behave differently in dev, test, and prod without separate codebases.

How they combine:

- Auto-configuration wires JPA, transactions, and pooling once `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` is present.
- `@Profile` then swaps the environment-specific beans on top.
- `spring.profiles.active` picks which profile is live.

A typical setup: Boot auto-configures the JPA stack, while `@Profile("dev")` picks H2 and `@Profile("prod")` picks Postgres.

The nuance: they're complementary, not rivals. One sets up capabilities; the other chooses the variant.

> **The gotcha:** auto-config runs first. If you add a profile bean but don't account for the auto-configured one, they can clash.

sections.title: Auto-Configuration vs Profiles at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Auto-configuration|~Structural question|is the library present?|@ConditionalOnClass / OnBean|wires the framework
blue|Profiles|~Environmental question|which environment am I in?|@Profile + spring.profiles.active|picks the variant
emerald|They combine|~Layers, not rivals|auto-config sets defaults|profiles override per env|both at startup
violet|Typical setup|~JPA auto-configured|@Profile("dev") H2 bean|@Profile("prod") Postgres bean|same app, different DBs

sections.title: Auto-Configuration vs Profiles
sections.content:
| Aspect | Auto-Configuration | Profiles |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | Classpath content and bean presence | Active environment set by property |
| Conditions | ConditionalOnClass, ConditionalOnBean, ConditionalOnProperty | at-Profile annotation with environment name |
| Purpose | Structural setup — what capabilities to enable | Environment-specific customization — which variant to use |
| When evaluated | Startup, based on available libraries | Startup, based on spring.profiles.active property |
| Example use | Create DataSource if JDBC driver exists | Use H2 in dev profile, Postgres in prod profile |

sections.title: Auto-Configuration Plus Profiles Working Together
When to Use Each
sections.content:
Use **auto-configuration** when you want automatic setup based on dependencies. If you add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa, you want JPA auto-configured without manual bean definitions.

Use **ConditionalOnClass** in custom auto-configurations when creating reusable libraries.

Use **profiles** when you need different behavior in different environments. In dev you want an embedded H2 database, in prod you want a production Postgres instance.

Use at-Profile on configuration classes or bean methods. **Combine them** when you need both: let auto-configuration handle the complex setup (like transaction management, connection pooling) and use profiles to provide environment-specific properties (database URL, credentials, pool sizes). Common pattern: application.properties has shared settings, application-dev.properties and application-prod.properties have environment-specific overrides, and custom beans use at-Profile to switch implementations entirely.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Conflating profiles with auto-configuration**: Freshers think at-Profile is the same as ConditionalOnClass or try to use auto-configuration conditions to switch between dev and prod, not realizing profiles are specifically for environment-based switching.
- **Creating duplicate auto-configurations**: Freshers copy entire auto-configuration classes and add at-Profile, duplicating Spring Boot's work instead of just customizing the specific beans they need per environment.
- **Not understanding the evaluation order**: Auto-configuration runs first, then profile-specific beans can override. Freshers create a profile-specific bean but forget that auto-configuration already created one, causing conflicts because they didn't exclude the auto-configured bean properly.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Auto-configuration**: structural bean creation based on classpath and bean presence, uses ConditionalOnClass and ConditionalOnBean annotations
- **Profiles**: environment-based bean creation, controlled by spring.profiles.active property and at-Profile annotation
- **Complementary mechanisms**: auto-configuration provides default setup, profiles customize per environment (dev, test, prod)
- **Set active profile**: use spring.profiles.active property in application.properties or command-line argument (--spring.profiles.active=dev)
- **Profile-specific properties**: application-dev.properties automatically loads when dev profile is active, overriding application.properties
- **Combining both**: common pattern is auto-configuration handles complex setup, profiles provide environment-specific configurations like database URLs
- **Override auto-configured beans**: use at-Profile on custom beans to replace auto-configured defaults in specific environments without disabling the entire auto-configuration

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Auto-configuration and profiles solve different problems but work together. Auto-configuration is about structural setup — it activates beans based on what's on your classpath and what beans already exist. It uses conditions like ConditionalOnClass to say if you have the H2 database driver, I'll create a DataSource automatically. Profiles are about environment-specific configuration — they activate beans based on which environment you're running in like dev, test, or prod. You mark beans with at-Profile dev and they only get created when the dev profile is active. You set the active profile with spring dot profiles dot active in application dot properties or as a command-line argument. Here's how they work together in practice. Let's say you're building a REST API with a database. Spring Boot's auto-configuration sees the spring-boot-starter-data-jpa dependency and automatically sets up JPA, transaction management, and connection pooling. That's the same in all environments. Now you want different databases per environment — H2 embedded in dev, Postgres in prod. You'd create a configuration class with two at-Bean methods, both returning DataSource. One has at-Profile dev and creates an H2 DataSource. The other has at-Profile prod and creates a Postgres DataSource. Auto-configuration handles the complex JPA setup, profiles handle the environment-specific database choice. Another example: you might use ConditionalOnProperty for feature flags that apply across all environments, but at-Profile for switching entire service implementations like a mock email service in dev versus the real SendGrid integration in prod. One mistake freshers make is thinking these are competing approaches and trying to do everything with just profiles or just auto-configuration. In reality you want auto-configuration for the heavy lifting and profiles for the last-mile environment customization. They're complementary layers.

speakable_v2.hook: Auto-configuration and profiles solve different problems. They work best when you use them together.
